steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Finn Bartlett had tended the Rustfall Point Lighthouse for thirteen years, ever since he’d answered the old seafarer’s ad in the harbor tavern. The squat, white tower perched on a jagged cliff overlooking the North Sea, its lantern room a small beacon of warmth against wind-driven slate skies. Each night Finn climbed the narrow spiral stairs with a lantern in hand, polished the Fresnel lens, and trimmed the wick of the oil lamp. He took pride in the perfect arc of light that swept across the black waves, guiding ships safely around hidden reefs.

One autumn evening, a storm cuffed the lighthouse with gale-force winds and driving spray. Finn secured the railings, tied down his dog-eared logbook, and lit the lamp as the first wave thundered against the cliff. Hours passed in near darkness between lashing gusts. By midnight, he caught sight of a fishing cutter’s lantern, its beam faint and struggling against rain. Finn rang the fog bell in rhythmic tolls, his hands raw from cold, hoping the sailors would hear. When he finally glimpsed the boat drawing slowly into calmer waters, relief flooded him. Though his body shivered, his spirit shone brighter than the lamp above.

When dawn broke, Finn climbed outside one last time to admire the dawn-pink horizon. The cutter, battered but seaworthy, bobbed safely in the bay below. He watched the fishermen wave in thanks before their vessel turned toward open sea. Back inside, Finn squeezed the oil lamp’s wick, secured his tools, and jotted a single line in his log: “Tonight, the light held true.” Then he paused, brushing a lock of windblown hair from his brow, and smiled. In the quiet after the storm, he felt more than a keeper of light—he was a guardian of hope.
